claims.claim: The page explains what happens when federal appropriations lapse
claims.sourceSpan: When a funding gap occurs, federal agencies are generally required to begin a shutdown of the affected projects and activities, which includes the prompt furlough of non-excepted personnel.

claims.claim: A shutdown follows a funding gap: appropriations for a project or activity not enacted in time
claims.sourceSpan: If there is an interval during a fiscal year when appropriations for a particular project or activity are not enacted into law, either in the form of a regular appropriations act or a CR, a funding gap (also referred to as a funding lapse) may occur.

claims.claim: The Antideficiency Act is the requirement that forces agencies to stop
claims.sourceSpan: make or authorize an expenditure or obligation exceeding an amount available in an appropriation or fund for the expenditure or obligation

claims.claim: The gaps have lasted a measurable range of durations
claims.sourceSpan: Since FY1977, 23 funding gaps have occurred, ranging in duration from 1 day to 75 full days.

claims.claim: A funding gap is an interval when appropriations for a project or activity are not enacted, as a regular act or a CR
claims.sourceSpan: If there is an interval during a fiscal year when appropriations for a particular project or activity are not enacted into law, either in the form of a regular appropriations act or a CR, a funding gap (also referred to as a funding lapse) may occur.

claims.claim: When a gap occurs agencies are generally required to begin a shutdown, including prompt furlough of non-excepted personnel
claims.sourceSpan: When a funding gap occurs, federal agencies are generally required to begin a shutdown of the affected projects and activities, which includes the prompt furlough of non-excepted personnel.

claims.claim: A gap and a shutdown are distinct events
claims.sourceSpan: Although a shutdown may be the result of a funding gap, the two events should be distinguished.

claims.claim: OMB has indicated a shutdown within the first day of a gap may be postponed if resolution appears imminent
claims.sourceSpan: the Office of Management and Budget has previously indicated that a shutdown of agency operations within the first day of the funding gap may be postponed if a resolution appears to be imminent

claims.claim: Many funding gaps since FY1977 did not result in shutdowns
claims.sourceSpan: Many of the funding gaps that have occurred since FY1977 do not appear to have resulted in "shutdowns."

claims.claim: More than one funding gap can occur in a single fiscal year
claims.sourceSpan: Multiple funding gaps may occur within a fiscal year.

claims.sourceSpan: Except as specified in this subchapter or any other provision of law, an officer or employee of the United States Government or of the District of Columbia government may not

claims.claim: The prohibition covers expenditures or obligations exceeding an amount available in an appropriation or fund
claims.sourceSpan: make or authorize an expenditure or obligation exceeding an amount available in an appropriation or fund for the expenditure or obligation

claims.claim: It also covers contracts or obligations for payment before an appropriation is made, unless authorized by law
claims.sourceSpan: involve either government in a contract or obligation for the payment of money before an appropriation is made unless authorized by law

claims.sourceSpan: may not accept voluntary services for either government or employ personal services exceeding that authorized by law except for emergencies involving the safety of human life or the protection of property

claims.claim: The emergencies exception excludes ongoing, regular functions whose suspension would not imminently threaten life or property
claims.sourceSpan: does not include ongoing, regular functions of government the suspension of which would not imminently threaten the safety of human life or the protection of property

claims.sourceSpan: The federal fiscal year runs from October 1 to September 30.

claims.sourceSpan: the term "excepted employee" means an excepted employee or an employee performing emergency work, as such terms are defined by the Office of Personnel Management or the appropriate District of Columbia public employer, as applicable

claims.claim: In executive-branch usage excepted covers both the activities that must continue and the employees who are not furloughed
claims.sourceSpan: In the executive branch, and in the context of a funding gap, the term "excepted" may refer to (1) the government activities that must continue during a funding gap and (2) the federal employees who are not furloughed and who must continue to come to work during a funding gap.

claims.claim: News media sometimes use essential instead of excepted
claims.sourceSpan: News media sometimes use the term "essential" instead of "excepted."

claims.claim: It has since disappeared from official executive-branch use in favour of excepted

claims.claim: REMOVED, F-FAIL (sweep, independently re-confirmed): the meta description and the opening sentence both defined a shutdown as occurring "when Congress fails to pass appropriations legislation ... and the President signs a continuing resolution or full-year spending bill to restore it" - asserting the failure and the cure inside one "occurs when" clause. The definition turns on non-enactment. Replaced with the CRS funding-gap definition (R47106), the CRS consequence (RS20348), and the gap/shutdown distinction the original never made.

REMOVED, F-FAIL found by this audit rather than the sweep, which graded it only F-UNSOURCED: "The longest shutdown in U.S. history ran 35 days, from December 22, 2018 to January 25, 2019, stemming from a dispute over border wall funding." Two errors. (1) CRS RS20348 counts that gap at 34 FULL days and dates its start to the expiration of P.L. 115-298 at midnight on December 21, 2018. (2) It is no longer the longest: RS20348, updated May 26, 2026, records an FY2026 gap of 42 full days ending November 12, 2025 and a third FY2026 gap of 75 full days ending April 30, 2026. The claim was already false when this page published on 2026-05-08. The border-wall causation had no source and is gone; the section now reports the CRS table.

REMOVED, F-FAIL (sweep): the page split one legal category into two labels, calling functions "essential" in one paragraph while calling military personnel "excepted" two paragraphs earlier. The operative term in 31 U.S.C. 1341(c)(1)(D) and in OMB Circular A-11 section 124 is EXCEPTED, and A-11 uses "exempt" for a different thing - functions financed by appropriations that have not lapsed. The page now states the statutory term, the four A-11 excepted categories, and the excepted/exempt distinction.

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED (sweep; the appropriations batch removed the same claim from its pages): "Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, SNAP (food stamps), and other entitlement programs operate under permanent appropriations - they do not require annual funding bills to continue. Benefit checks keep going out during shutdowns." CRS RL34680 says the opposite in kind: such programs "may, or may not, be affected by a funding gap. Specific circumstances appear to be significant," because the payments may be processed by annually funded staff. Replaced with the CRS statement and the SSA FY1996 worked example.

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED: "Active-duty military personnel are required to report for duty during a shutdown as a matter of law ... In past shutdowns, military pay has sometimes been delayed by days." No stored or fetched source states either half as a general rule. What CRS RL34680 records is narrower and specific to FY2014 - the Pay Our Military Act, an automatic CR enacted September 30, 2013. Rather than restate a general rule off one special statute, the paragraph is gone.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "federal contractors, by contrast, generally do not receive compensation for work time lost during a shutdown." The only thing in the stored sources is a dated FY1996 report that "employees of federal contractors reportedly were furloughed without pay" - an instance, not a rule, and about contractor employees rather than contractors. Removed rather than narrowed.

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED (sweep): the agency-by-agency list (Transportation, HUD, parts of Justice, the IRS during filing seasons, the FDA, parts of Agriculture, national parks, federal museums) and the follow-on paragraph on what stops inside an agency ("websites may go dark", "told not to report to work or check email"). Nothing stored supports the list, and agency-level outcomes turn on each agency lapse plan, which A-11 requires each agency to publish. Replaced with the sourced excepted-function categories and the 1981 Stockman list of continuing activities.

REMOVED, F-FAIL: "Agency general counsel offices issue 'shutdown plans' well in advance of anticipated lapses." OMB Circular A-11 section 124.2 assigns that to AGENCY HEADS, in consultation with their general counsels, and requires an up-to-date lapse plan on file with OMB rather than plans issued at the counsel-office level. Corrected against the circular.

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED: "When appropriations lapse at midnight on September 30 ... most agencies must immediately stop spending." Two problems. Gaps do not only start on October 1 - RS20348 records that 15 of the 23 gaps since FY1977 began more than one day into the fiscal year - and "immediately" is contradicted by the OMB first-day postponement RS20348 also records. Replaced with the fiscal-year dates from R47106 and the CRS account of what actually follows a gap.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "Shutdowns are always the result of a breakdown in the appropriations process. They are not accidents"; "Most resolve within days because the political pressure - on both parties, from constituent complaints and economic disruption - becomes too large to sustain"; "Shorter shutdowns have lasted hours or a weekend"; "The duration varies enormously." Unsourced causal and behavioural assertions. The duration section now reports the CRS table, including the sourced fact that about half the gaps lasted three days or less.

REMOVED, F-FAIL (sweep): "Typically, back pay is authorized in the same legislation" and "though they typically receive back pay once the shutdown ends." Since the Government Employee Fair Treatment Act of 2019, 31 U.S.C. 1341(c)(2) makes back pay a standing requirement for any lapse beginning on or after December 22, 2018 - not a discretionary term of the bill that ends the lapse. The pre-2019 practice is now stated separately and dated.

CORRECTED BY THIS AUDIT, no sweep flag: my own first draft of the replacement text attributed the list of continuing activities to "guidance OMB issued ahead of the FY2014 shutdown." CRS RL34680 attributes it to an OMB memorandum of November 17, 1981 from Director David A. Stockman, which was merely still in effect for FY1996 and posted by OPM for FY2014. ROUND 1 hostile Sonnet source-only pass: 2 BLOCKING, 7 ADVISORY. Both blocking findings ACCEPTED after my own fresh source read, neither on the agent's word. (1) My replacement H2 asserted "Federal shutdown law does not use the word essential." That is false, and the page's own quoted source proves it: the 1981 Stockman memo is headed "Conduct essential activities to the extent that they protect life and property," and CRS RL34680 Box 3 sets out the real position - news media use "essential" for "excepted", the executive branch did too in the early 1980s, and it has since disappeared from official use "in part to prevent a colloquial interpretation of the term essential as referring to relative importance or value." The section is rebuilt on Box 3 and now adds the OPM "exempt" definition and the caveat that executive-branch terminology does not officially bind the other two branches. (2) "the Government Employee Fair Treatment Act of 2019" was an out-of-source proper noun - zero hits across all six registered sources, grep-confirmed. Replaced with what the statute itself records: subsection (c) added by Pub. L. 116-1, enacted January 16, 2019. Advisories accepted and fixed: the invented "Then:" sequencing in section 124.3 (the source's order is the reverse); the circular "defines an excepted employee as one who means..."; the unsourced "usually described as the longest" framing; the FY1996 and FY2014 rows of Table 1 added on the advisory that the duration section named only FY2019 before 2026; and three coverage gaps now carrying ledger rows. The advisory that the JSON-LD carried no dateModified was also accepted and fixed - without that field publish-article --refresh aborts on read-back.

ROUND 2 hostile Sonnet pass, fresh agent, no edits made during the round: 2 BLOCKING, 7 ADVISORY. Both blocking findings ACCEPTED after my own fresh source read.
